title: The Height Rule Hall
covers: how to turn "at least", "no more than", "more than" and "less than" rules into inequalities, test values, and show them on a number line

intro.caption: Lesson 8-4 — writing inequalities. Every ride at Screamline Park has a rule sign. Mr. Krank loves rules so much that he made a game show about them: The Height Rule Hall. Tonight Hana faces Gus, who has never read a ride sign in his life.

balloons.t: Welcome to the Height Rule Hall! Break a rule, lose the game.
Rules. Love them. Never follow them.

pages.ch: Chapter 1 · Gus Reads a Sign (Sort Of)

balloons.t: The Screamer says "at least 48 inches." I'm 47. Close enough!
"At least 48" means 48 or MORE. 47 is not in.

pages.caption: An inequality compares two sides with <, >, ≤ or ≥. "At least" means ≥, so the number itself counts. "No more than" means ≤.

balloons.t: Round one. Turn the sign into math. Let h be the rider's height.
Put each height in the rule. True? You ride. False? You watch me eat.
And 48 counts! "At least" includes the number on the sign.

pages.caption: Every value that makes an inequality true is a solution. All of them together make the solution set.

balloons.t: Closed circle if the number counts. Open circle if it doesn't. The ray points to the riders who fit.
Final question! Three parts. Miss one, and the trophy goes to the raccoon.
Wait. Can I wear the trophy as a hat?
I didn't ride the Screamer. But I won a trophy!

win.caption: "At least" means ≥ and "no more than" means ≤: the number counts, so the circle is closed. "More than" means > and "less than" means <: the number does not count, so the circle is open.

gates.title: Round 1 · Write the Rule
gates.prompt: Turn each ride sign into an inequality.
hints: Conceptual: "at least" means that number or more, so it includes the number: ≥. "No more than" means that number or less, so it also includes it: ≤.
Procedural: put the letter first. Ask: can the rider be bigger or smaller than the number? Does the number itself count?

steps: Practice sign: "At least 40 tokens to win." Let t be the tokens.
worked.q: Write "no more than 5 scoops" with s.

items.q: The Screamer: "Riders must be at least 48 inches tall." Which inequality fits the height h?

options.fb: That leaves out 48. A rider who is exactly 48 inches CAN ride, so use ≥.
Wrong direction. ≤ means 48 or less, which is "at most." Taller riders can ride.
That is the riders who CAN'T ride. It also leaves out 48.

items.q: The Spin Cups: "No more than 6 riders per cup." Which inequality fits the number of riders r?

options.fb: That leaves out 6. Six riders is allowed, so use ≤.
Wrong direction. ≥ means 6 or more. "No more than" means 6 or fewer.
That is too many riders. It is the wrong direction and leaves out 6.

gates.pass: h ≥ 48 and r ≤ 6. DING! Hana takes the lead. Gus buzzes in late with "h is for head."

gates.title: Round 2 · Test the Riders
gates.prompt: Put each value into the rule. If the statement is true, the value is a solution.
hints: Conceptual: an inequality has many solutions. Any value that makes it true is one of them.
Procedural: replace the letter with the value. Read the statement out loud, like "52 ≥ 48." Is it true?

steps: Test 5: 5 ≤ 5 is true. Test 3: 3 ≤ 5 is true.
Test 6: 6 ≤ 5 is false. So 5 and 3 are solutions, and 6 is not.

items.q: The Screamer rule is h ≥ 48. Tap every height that can ride.

options.fb: 47 ≥ 48 is false. 47 is less than 48, so this rider waits.

items.fbMiss: You left out a rider who can ride. Remember: ≥ includes 48 itself, and every height above it.
items.fbExtra: One of those heights is too short. Test it: is it 48 or more?

items.q: The Drop Zone rule for bags is w ≤ 10 pounds. Which bag is NOT allowed?

options.fb: 10 ≤ 10 is true. ≤ includes 10, so this bag is allowed.
7 ≤ 10 is true. Lighter bags are allowed.
9.5 ≤ 10 is true. It is less than 10, so it is allowed.

gates.pass: 48 and 52 can ride, and the 12-pound bag stays behind. Bandit tries to sneak it on anyway.

gates.title: Round 3 · Paint the Signs
gates.prompt: Rafi paints a number line on every sign. Place the circle, pick open or closed, and point the ray.
hints: Conceptual: a closed circle means the number is a solution (≥ or ≤). An open circle means it is not (> or <).
Procedural: tap the number from the rule. Choose closed for ≥ or ≤. Point the ray right for bigger values, left for smaller values.

steps: 40 counts, so draw a closed circle at 40.
"Or more" means bigger numbers, so the ray points right.
worked.q: For s ≤ 5, what circle do you draw and which way does the ray point?
worked.a: A closed circle at 5, ray pointing left.

fb.msg: 47 is Gus's height, not the rule. The rule starts at 48.
That starts at 49 and leaves out 48. Put the circle on 48.

items.fbDefault: Put the circle on the number in the rule: 48.
items.fbClosed: An open circle leaves out 48. "At least 48" includes 48, so use a closed circle.
items.fbOpen: This rule does not include its number, so use an open circle.
items.fbDir: ≥ means 48 or MORE. Taller riders are bigger numbers, so point the ray right.

items.q: The Kiddie Train sign: riders no more than 42 inches. Show h ≤ 42.

fb.msg: That leaves out 42. A rider who is exactly 42 inches can ride. Put the circle on 42.

items.fbDefault: Put the circle on the number in the rule: 42.
items.fbClosed: "No more than 42" includes 42, so the circle is closed.
items.fbOpen: This rule does not include its number, so use an open circle.
items.fbDir: ≤ means 42 or LESS. Shorter riders are smaller numbers, so point the ray left.

gates.pass: Two new signs hang at the rides. Gus reads one out loud. Correctly. The crowd gasps.

gates.title: Final Question · Krank's Last Rule
gates.prompt: Three parts. Write the rule, test a rider, and paint the sign.
hints: Conceptual: "more than" and "less than" do not include the number (> and <). "At least" and "no more than" do (≥ and ≤).
Procedural: write the rule with the letter first, test the value by substituting, then use an open circle for > or <.

steps: Practice: "More than 30 points wins a badge." Let p be the points.
"More than 30" does not include 30, so the rule is p > 30.
On a number line: an open circle at 30 and a ray to the right.

items.q: Part 1 · Hana's prize booth: "You need more than 20 tickets for a big prize." Which rule fits the tickets t?

options.fb: That includes 20. "More than 20" means 20 is NOT enough, so use >.
Wrong direction. < means fewer than 20 tickets.
Wrong direction, and it includes 20. You need MORE than 20.

items.q: Part 2 · The Mega Drop rule is h ≥ 52. Gus is 47 inches tall. Can he ride?

options.t: Yes — the mascot head makes him taller
options.fb: Nice try, Gus. Measure the rider, not the head: 47 ≥ 52 is false.

items.q: Part 3 · Paint the prize sign: show t > 20.

fb.msg: The circle goes on the number in the rule, 20. An open circle there shows 20 is not included.

items.fbDefault: Put the circle on the number in the rule: 20.
items.fbOpen: 20 tickets is NOT more than 20. Use an open circle to leave 20 out.
items.fbClosed: This rule includes its number, so use a closed circle.
items.fbDir: "More than" means bigger numbers, so point the ray right.

gates.pass: t > 20, "no" for Gus, and an open circle at 20. The board lights up. Hana and Gus win as a team.

journal.heading: Lesson 8-4 — what the Height Rule Hall taught us
rows: A math sentence that compares with <, >, ≤ or ≥. It has many solutions, not just one.
"At least 48" is h ≥ 48. "No more than 6" is r ≤ 6. The number counts, so the circle is closed.
"More than 20" is t > 20. The number does not count, so the circle is open.
Substitute it. 52 ≥ 48 is true, so 52 can ride. 47 ≥ 48 is false, so 47 waits.
Pointing the ray the wrong way, or leaving out the number on the sign. Read the words, then pick the symbol.
journal.quote: "No more than one funnel cake per raccoon. I read that as 'at least.'" — Bandit

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 8-4 (Write and Represent Inequalities) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: translating at least, no more than, more than and less than into inequality symbols, testing values, and showing a rule on a number line.
standards: Write an inequality to represent a constraint or condition; recognize that inequalities have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions on number line diagrams
